label: prf:polynomial-bar-involution
title: Proof of polynomial bar involution
html:
By definition \overline p := p.\mathrm{comp}(-X); applying to p = X gives X.\mathrm{comp}(-X) = -X. \square

Proposition. \overline{-X} = X. Proof. (-X).\mathrm{comp}(-X) = -(X.\mathrm{comp}(-X)) = -(-X) = X, since composition commutes with negation and -(-X) = X. \square

Proposition. \overline{C c} = C c. Proof. Constants are bar-fixed: (C c).\mathrm{comp}(-X) = C c, since substitution does not affect constants. \square

Proposition. \overline{p+q} = \overline p + \overline q. Proof. Composition distributes over addition: (p+q).\mathrm{comp}(r) = p.\mathrm{comp}(r) + q.\mathrm{comp}(r). \square

Proposition. \overline{p \cdot q} = \overline p \cdot \overline q. Proof. Composition distributes over multiplication: (p q).\mathrm{comp}(r) = p.\mathrm{comp}(r) \cdot q.\mathrm{comp}(r). \square

Proposition. \overline 1 = 1 and \overline 0 = 0. Proof. The constants 1 and 0 are unchanged by substitution. \square

Proposition. \overline{\overline p} = p. Proof. (p.\mathrm{comp}(-X)).\mathrm{comp}(-X) = p.\mathrm{comp}((-X).\mathrm{comp}(-X)) = p.\mathrm{comp}(X) = p, by associativity of composition, \overline{-X} = X, and p.\mathrm{comp}(X) = p. \square

Power identities

Proposition. \overline{X^2} = X^2. Proof. X^2 = X \cdot X, so \overline{X^2} = \overline X \cdot \overline X = (-X)(-X) = X^2. \square

Proposition. \overline{X^n} = (-1)^n \cdot X^n. Proof. Induction on n. Base (n=0): \overline 1 = 1. Step: \overline{X^{k+1}} = \overline{X \cdot X^k} = (-X) \cdot (-1)^k X^k = (-1)^{k+1} X^{k+1}. \square

Proposition. \overline{X^{2n}} = X^{2n}. Proof. From the power identity \overline{X^n} = (-1)^n X^n: coefficient is (-1)^{2n} = ((-1)^2)^n = 1. \square

Proposition. \overline{X^{2n+1}} = -X^{2n+1}. Proof. From the power identity \overline{X^n} = (-1)^n X^n: coefficient is (-1)^{2n+1} = -1. \square

Scalar identities

Proposition. Every natural-number scalar is bar-fixed in R[X]. Proof. Induction on n. Base: \overline 0 = 0. Step: \overline{k+1} = \overline k + \overline 1 = k + 1. \square

Proposition. \overline{p - q} = \overline p - \overline q. Proof. p - q = p + (-1) \cdot q; bar commutes with + and \cdot, and \overline{-1} = -1 (composition commutes with negation and fixes 1). \square

Proposition. \overline{-p} = -\overline p. Proof. Take p = 0 in the subtraction identity: \overline{-q} = \overline{0 - q} = 0 - \overline q = -\overline q. \square

Concrete bar-symmetric polynomials

Proposition. \overline{4 + X^2} = 4 + X^2. Proof. \overline 4 = 4 since natural-number scalars are bar-fixed (with 4 = (4:\mathbb{N})); \overline{X^2} = X^2; combine by additivity. \square

Proposition. The polynomial c_5^{[6]}(X) := -\tfrac{5}{4} - \tfrac{X^2}{16} + \tfrac{X^4}{64} - \tfrac{X^6}{256} is bar-symmetric. Proof. Every term has the form C(c) \cdot X^{2k} with c \in \mathbb{R} and k \in \{0,1,2,3\}. Constants are bar-fixed; even powers are bar-fixed. Sum and difference of bar-symmetric is bar-symmetric. \square

Proposition. \cos^{[6]}(X) := 1 - X^2/2 + X^4/24 - X^6/720 and \cosh^{[6]}(X) := 1 + X^2/2 + X^4/24 + X^6/720 are bar-symmetric. Proof. Same structure as the previous proposition for c_5^{[6]}: each term C(c) \cdot X^{2k} with bar-fixed coefficient and bar-fixed even power. \square

Theorem. All three layer truncations — series c_5^{[6]}, phase \cos^{[6]}, gain \cosh^{[6]} — are bar-symmetric in the same polynomial ring \mathbb{R}[X] under the same bar-involution X \mapsto -X. Proof. Conjunction of the three propositions above. The three layer avatars live in the same ambient ring with the same bar — this is the categorical-derivation unification at the truncated-polynomial level. \square

Pre-archimedean generic versions

Proposition. Over any commutative ring R (no field needed), the polynomial c_0 + c_1 X^2 + c_2 X^4 + c_3 X^6 is bar-symmetric for arbitrary c_0, c_1, c_2, c_3 \in R. Proof. Per-term: C(c_i) is bar-fixed as a constant; X^{2k} is bar-fixed as an even power. The sum is bar-symmetric by additivity. No archimedean structure invoked. \square

Theorem. For any n \in \mathbb{N} and any c : \mathbb{N} \to R, the polynomial P_n(X) := \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} c_k X^{2k} is bar-symmetric. Proof. Induction on n. Base: empty sum = 0 bar-symmetric. Step: P_{k+1} = P_k + C(c_k) X^{2k}; IH gives P_k bar-symmetric, per-term argument gives C(c_k) X^{2k} bar-symmetric; sum bar-symmetric. Holds for arbitrary truncation degree over any CommRing. \square

Theorem. Sums of odd-power monomials with arbitrary R-coefficients are bar-anti-symmetric. Proof. Induction analogous to even case, using \overline{X^{2n+1}} = -X^{2n+1} to flip sign on each term. \square

Evaluations

Proposition. c_5^{[6]}(0) = -5/4. Proof. All positive-degree terms vanish at X = 0; constant term is -5/4. \square

Proposition. c_5^{[6]}(1) = -333/256. Proof. -5/4 - 1/16 + 1/64 - 1/256 = -320/256 - 16/256 + 4/256 - 1/256 = -333/256. Approximates exact c_5(1) = -13/10 = -332.8/256 with relative error \approx 0.06\% (consistent with O(X^8 / 4^4) Taylor truncation at X = 1). \square

Future extensions: the rational-function field \mathrm{Frac}(R[X]), for rational-function functors realising the proved closed form c_5 = -3/2 + 1/(X^2 + 4), and the formal power-series ring R[[X]], for the formal power-series limit of the truncated avatars.
